newsitem.title: GREECE: GREENPEACE ACTIVISTS ACQUITTED FOR REFINERY ACTION.
newsitem.headline: GREENPEACE ACTIVISTS ACQUITTED FOR REFINERY ACTION.

text.p: A Greek court acquitted on Friday 17 Greek and foreign Greenpeace activists charged over a 24-hour blockade of a major oil refinery near the Corinth canal to protest over oil pollution.

The three-member court in the southern Greek city of Corinth found eight Greek and nine foreign defendants not guilty of trespass or hindering a public service company, charges that carry a five-year prison term.

The court found David Enever, captain of the Greenpeace ship Arctic Sunrise that helped blockade the Motor Oil refinery in November, guilty of disobedience for refusing to obey coast guard orders to move his ship away from the facilities.
The Briton was sentenced to four months in jail but he appealed his conviction and was released.
"David Enever was found guilty of disobedience, with the mitigating factor that his motives were noble," the presiding judge said. "All other defendants are found innocent of all charges."

The activists took over the refinery's port to protest over a major spill at its docking facilities in August. They were forcibly removed by coast guard commandos, who cut through chains pinning them to mooring buoys and loading cranes.
An estimated 300 tonnes of crude oil was spilled as a tanker owned by Motor Oil was unloading during a thunderstorm in the middle of the night.
Motor Oil has rejected accusations that its safety measures are lax, saying they were beyond those required by Greek law, and blamed the accident on the sudden storm.

Initial reports said a lightning bolt struck dead a worker and the ship was detached from its moorings, breaking its loading pipe. But in pressing charges against Motor Oil, a judicial council said the ship was not properly docked and its mooring ropes had been loose.
Motor Oil, jointly owned by Saudi Aramco and the Greek Vardinoyannis family, was fined 150 million drachmas ($650,000) by the Merchant Marine Ministry for the accident.

The refinery's director, the loading manager, the captain of the ship and the first mate have been charged with causing serious marine oil pollution because of negligence and face up to five years in jail if convicted.
Greenpeace has said it was a paradox that its activists would be charged and tried so soon after the November action while Motor Oil was still unpunished for the August oil spill.

"This is the first time Greenpeace is tried in Greece and the winner is not only Greenpeace but Greek justice as well. It must keep up the good work with a swift trial of Motor Oil," said Nikos Charalambidis, a defendant and leader of the Greenpeace refinery action.

Greenpeace wants a ban on loading at night or in bad weather, stricter laws against oil pollution and more prevention measures. It says oil dispersants used after oil spills in Greece are toxic and should be forbidden.
